quotes.text: There were frequently live music programmes on all day, a big band interpreting different styles of Brazilian music like samba, bolero, baião or foxtrot.
I listened sometimes, fell in love with the music and started borrowing my sister's practice books.
While I read the lines, I listened to how the notes written on the instruments sounded and how they were grouped. That's how I learned how this music worked.
I already knew then: I wanted to become a musical arranger. However, there was not a single course available in the whole of Rio. So I decided to work towards my goal on my own.

The record company people approached me and asked me if I wanted to record an album. I was thrilled, but wanted to have full control over the creative process, that was my only demand – besides twelve violins, four violas, various cellos, a trumpet and a saxophone, as well as a trombone, two drums, a piano and a guitar.
A good arrangement is what makes the music grow and become bigger.
However, it wasn't my intention to sell millions of copies anyway. I just wanted to make my music without anyone from the outside interfering.
I was sad because my work was not recognised. By now I know I did what I was supposed to do. And I don't regret a thing.
The money was good, but I knew that no one in that milieu was interested in the music I was making. I guess that's why I stayed there. I wanted to flee from myself.
I'm still grateful to these people. They made my work known later on.

It was made during tough times in Brazil, when many lyrics were censored by the dictatorship. So, to avoid problems, Vitor had to use a lot of metaphors in the lyrics. 'Presente de Grego' meant that the dictatorship was a Trojan horse to Brazil, a bad gift. And 'Pelas Sombras' was about the way the government secret police acted in the shadows, hidden from public, getting people arrested. It was like camouflaging our feelings. But for me, I just wanted to make the best music I could.
